entities.summary:
Alexander Agricola was a Netherlandish composer of the Renaissance writing in the Franco-Flemish style, a prominent member of the Grande chapelle, the Habsburg musical establishment. Born in 1456 in Bruges, Flanders, Agricola was a renowned composer in the years around 1500, and his music was widely distributed throughout Europe. He composed music in all of the important sacred and secular styles of the time, including mass settings, motets, and chansons.

Agricola's significance lies in his contribution to the development of European music during the Renaissance. His compositions showcase the Franco-Flemish style, which blended elements of Flemish and French music. Agricola's music was performed in royal courts, churches, and monasteries throughout Europe, including the Habsburg Empire, the Holy Roman Empire, and the Kingdom of France.

Agricola's legacy can be seen in the works of later composers, such as Palestrina and Lasso, who were influenced by his compositions. His music also reflects the cultural exchange between Europe and the Mediterranean, where he spent time in Italy and France.

In 1506, Agricola died in Venice, leaving behind a body of work that continues to be studied and performed today.

Agricola's compositions include the 'Missa de nobilitate,' 'Missa prolationum,' and 'Missa super cantum.' His music has been published in several editions, including the 'Musica Dei Proprietate Adamantis,' which contains his compositions for solo voice and instrumental accompaniment.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Agricola's compositions helped establish the Franco-Flemish style as a major force in European music during the Renaissance, and his music was widely distributed throughout Europe, influencing composers and musicians in various regions and courts. Agricola's legacy can be seen in the works of later composers, such as Palestrina and Lasso, who were influenced by his compositions.
